newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open weaker on strong Japan Tankan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open weaker on strong Japan Tankan.

text.p: Treasuries opened lower, depressed in tandem with the dollar on fears of higher Japanese interest rates after a robust Tankan report on Japanese manufacturing activity overnight, dealers said.
But losses were limited in front of a five-year note auction this afternoon, as well as durable goods data at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT and existing home sales at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.

"This market's got to get ready for the five-year," said Mead Briggs, head of proprietary trading at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "There was some overnight selling ... It could have been the Tankan scared them out of positions.
In early trade, the 30-year Treasury bond was off 8/32 at 98-28/32 to yield 7.71 percent. The 10-year note was off 7/32 at 101-13/32, yielding 6.43 percent.
Durable goods orders, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are expected to have risen 0.6 percent in May, following a 1.3 percent climb in April.
Existing home sales for May, at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, are seen rising to a 4.07 million unit annualized rate, from 4.06 million units previously.
The numbers today are seen as relatively insignificant, with the market discounting a steady Federal Reserve in July.

"The market has discounted the Fed out of this meeting, so we're actually sort of thinking about what's happening next meeting," Briggs said. "The data we're getting this week is sort of ho-hum, the real data starts next week with purchasing managers, car sales and employment."

The dollar fell a yen and a half overnight after the diffusion index of manufacturing companies, a key index of business confidence in the Tankan, came in at plus seven in June from plus two in the previous Tankan in March.
Consensus forcasts looked for the Bank of Japan report to come in around zero.
"It gives people the perception the BOJ could be raising rates by the end of the year," said Doug Burtnick, senior fixed income analyst at Technical Data.
"It takes away from some of the competitiveness of U.S. yields right now and could wash out the remaining guys who were involved in the yen carry trades," Burtnick said.
Results from the Treasury's $11.5 billion sale of five-year paper should show up in early afternoon.
Analysts said the market views the price of the issue, which was off 4/32 at 100-23/32, yielding 6.33 percent in early trade, as still a bit expensive before the auction.
"The market needs to price in a little more of a concession for the five-year note ... I think it's going to want to do the auction a little cheaper than this," Burtnick said.
Elsewhere, the three-year note was off 1/32 at 100-17/32, with a yield of 6.17 percent.
At the short end of the maturity spectrum, the three-month bill was off one basis point at 5.00 percent and the six-month bill was flat at 5.08 percent in early dealings.
